videos.title: Ed Mylett On Why You Quit Right Before It Works
videos.description:
One decision. One meeting. One more phone call.

That's how far away your life is from changing, and Ed Mylett thinks you keep telling yourself it's much further.

In this clip, Ed Mylett and Jay Shetty talk about the night Ed's father pulled the car over, cried, and said he'd try to get sober one more time, and the promise he made instead of the one Ed wanted to hear.

Ed argues the thing you're most ashamed of is the thing that qualifies you. Jay opens up about a month he couldn't walk and how he missed his own progress by staring at how far he still had to go. They get into why 95% of people run their lives out of memory instead of imagination, and how to tell whether the friends around you are pulling you backwards.

Learn about the piñata at a kid's birthday party that explains why most people quit right before the candy comes out, and why one more in the wrong direction can cost you everything you were building it for.

JAY'S DAILY WISDOM DELIVERED STRAIGHT TO YOUR INBOX
Join 900,000+ readers discovering how small daily shifts create big life change with my free newsletter. Subscribe https://news.jayshetty.me/subscribe

Chapters
0:00 — The great lie about how far away it is
1:02 — Jay's month of not being able to walk
1:49 — Why your brain starts finding the openings
2:33 — The night his father pulled the car over
3:01 — "I can't promise you that"
3:43 — The stranger who helped his dad get sober
4:32 — Why attachment to the outcome kills it
5:04 — Memory and history vs. vision and imagination
6:12 — What your friends talk about when you're together
7:34 — Nostalgia lies to you about the past
9:11 — When you didn't grow up believing you deserve it
10:55 — Comfort creates self-care, discomfort creates self-respect
12:15 — One more in the wrong direction
13:12 — The question to ask yourself now
15:17 — The piñata nobody thinks they broke

videos.title: How (and why) to build a personal API
videos.description: Maddie's API surfaces her coffee order, pet names, timezone, favorite snacks, and SF restaurant picks. The intended user was a human who wants to do something nice without pestering her. The more interesting version, as Claire pointed out, is an agent that hits the API, checks when Maddie is next in SF, and books her favorite restaurant automatically.

videos.title: Hacking an old pager with AI
videos.description: The route to get a tweet onto her pager runs through the Twitter API, a Cloudflare Worker, Resend, Gmail, and finally the pager's own email address.
